title: SUM Function
objectives: By the end you can total any list of numbers with SUM, using one range, several ranges, rows, columns and separate cells.
about: SUM adds up numbers. It is the most used function in Excel. You give it the cells to add, and it returns the total. The cells can be one range such as B2:B9, several ranges separated by commas, or single cells. SUM ignores empty cells and text, so a heading or a note inside the range does no harm. Negative numbers, such as refunds, reduce the total. Use SUM for takings, expenses, scores, and quantities. To use it, type =SUM(, select the cells, close the bracket, and press Enter. The total updates whenever a cell in the range changes.

examples.scenario: A market stall owner totals three days of takings.
examples.why: The range B2:B4 holds all three days. SUM adds them.

examples.scenario: A shop owner totals one product across three months.
examples.why: A range can run across a row as well as down a column.

examples.scenario: An accountant adds two separate blocks and skips the heading between them.
examples.why: Commas separate the ranges. The heading in A4 is not part of either one.

examples.scenario: A bookkeeper nets sales and refunds.
examples.why: A negative number is simply subtracted by the addition.

watch_out: SUM ignores text, including numbers stored as text. If a total looks too small, check for numbers that are left-aligned.
A subtotal inside the range is counted twice. Add only the subtotals, or leave them out.
One error value, such as #N/A, inside the range makes SUM show the same error.
recap: You can now total any layout of numbers with SUM. Next, AutoSum writes the SUM formula for you.

steps.prompt: A market stall's takings for the week are in B2:B8. Wednesday includes a refund, shown as a negative number. Work out the weekly total in B9.
hints: A total adds a whole list. Which function adds a range of cells?
SUM(range) adds every number in a range, including negative ones. A range uses a colon: B2:B8 means B2 through B8. Negative refunds simply reduce the total.
Type =SUM(B2:B8) in B9 and press Enter. Excel adds all seven days, and the refund of -30 reduces the total to 775.
steps.explanation: SUM adds every number in the range. The negative refund reduces the total, so no special handling is needed.

common_mistakes.message: That adds only Monday and Sunday. Use SUM with the whole range B2:B8.
The range stops at Saturday. Sunday is in B8.
Sunday was counted twice. SUM already includes B8.
COUNT counts how many days have takings, 7. SUM adds them up.

steps.prompt: A shop's sales for each product run across a row: January, February and March in B2:D2. Work out the quarter total for Widget in E2, ready to fill down to E5.
hints: The numbers run across a row, not down a column. How do you write a range across?
A range can run across a row: B2:D2 means B2, C2 and D2. SUM adds all three. Fill the formula down and each row adds its own months.
Type =SUM(B2:D2) in E2 and press Enter, then fill down to E5. Each product gets its own January to March total.
steps.explanation: A range can run across a row. Filling down moves it to the next row, so each product adds its own months.

common_mistakes.message: That adds the January column for every product. Add across the row, B2:D2.
February is missing. Use SUM with B2:D2.
March is missing. The range must reach column D.

steps.prompt: A budget lists fixed costs in B2:B4 and variable costs in B7:B9. A budget limit sits in B5 between them. Work out the total costs in B11, without counting the limit.
hints: The limit between the two blocks must not be added. How can SUM take two separate ranges?
SUM accepts several ranges separated by commas. Give it the fixed block and the variable block as two arguments, and it skips everything between them.
Type =SUM(B2:B4,B7:B9) in B11 and press Enter. The comma joins the two blocks, and the limit in B5 is left out. The total is 5700.
steps.explanation: Each comma-separated range is added, and anything between them is ignored.

common_mistakes.message: That includes the budget limit in B5. Add the two blocks separately.
That adds only the fixed costs. The variable costs are missing.
Transport in B9 is missing. The variable block runs to B9.

steps.prompt: Column B holds invoice amounts. One cell says n/a, and new invoices will be added below. In D2, total the amounts so new ones are included automatically.
hints: New rows will keep being added. How can a formula cover a whole column?
A whole column reference such as B:B includes every row, now and later. SUM ignores the heading and the text n/a, so only the amounts are added.
Type =SUM(B:B) in D2 and press Enter. Excel adds every number in column B and skips the heading and n/a. The total is 600.
steps.explanation: B:B means the whole column, so new invoices are added automatically. SUM ignores text such as the heading and n/a.

common_mistakes.message: That range stops at row 7, so new invoices below will be missed. Use the whole column, B:B.
That also stops at row 7. Use the whole column, B:B.
New invoices would be missed, and the formula is easy to get wrong. Use SUM(B:B).

steps.prompt: A sales sheet has an East block with its subtotal in B5 and a West block with its subtotal in B9. Work out the grand total in B10 without counting any sale twice.
hints: Each subtotal already includes its block. Which cells would double count if you add everything?
A SUM over the whole table adds each sale and then its subtotal, counting everything twice. Add only the two subtotals, or only the individual sales.
Type =SUM(B5,B9) in B10 and press Enter. It adds the East subtotal, 450, and the West subtotal, 300. The grand total is 750.
steps.explanation: A subtotal already contains its sales. Adding the subtotals alone, or the sales alone, avoids counting anything twice.

common_mistakes.message: That adds the sales and the subtotals, so everything is counted twice. Add only the subtotals.
That includes the East subtotal in B5 as well as its sales. Avoid double counting.
That adds the West sales and subtotal together. Add only B5 and B9.

title: AutoSum
objectives: By the end you can total columns, rows and whole tables with AutoSum, and use its arrow for Average, Count, Max and Min.
about: AutoSum is a shortcut that writes a SUM formula for you. Excel looks at the numbers next to the cell you pick and guesses the range to add. Press Alt+= and Excel suggests =SUM(...) with the range outlined. Press Enter to accept it. Select empty cells under or beside your data, and Alt+= totals every column or row at once. The AutoSum button on the Home tab has a small arrow with Average, Count Numbers, Max, and Min. Use it for quick totals under any table. Always check that the outlined range is the one you want.

shortcut_table.windows: Select data + empty row, then Alt+=
shortcut_table.mac: Select the same cells, then the Σ button

shortcut_table.windows: Select data + empty column, then Alt+=
shortcut_table.mac: Select the same cells, then the Σ button

shortcut_table.windows: Select cells and read Sum in the status bar

examples.scenario: A stall owner totals a column of takings.
examples.why: AutoSum outlines B2:B4 and Enter accepts it.

examples.scenario: A manager totals two branch columns together.
examples.why: The empty bottom row gets a total under each column.

examples.scenario: A shop owner totals each row of a small table.
examples.why: The empty column on the right gets a total for each row.

examples.scenario: A teacher finds an average without typing a formula.
examples.formula: Click A5, open the AutoSum arrow, choose Average, press Enter
examples.why: The arrow offers other summary functions.

watch_out: Check the outlined range before pressing Enter. AutoSum stops at the first empty cell above the one you picked.
With a block selected, AutoSum fills a total for every column or row that has an empty cell at its end.
In a web browser on a Mac, Cmd+Shift+T reopens a closed tab, so use the AutoSum button instead.
recap: You can now total whole tables in one step. Next, a summary lesson mixes SUM and AutoSum on new layouts.

steps.prompt: Daily takings are in B2:B8 and B9 is empty. You are in B9. Total the week with AutoSum, and accept the formula Excel suggests.
hints: Excel can guess the range for you. Which shortcut starts that?
AutoSum writes a SUM formula for you. Click the empty cell under the numbers and press Alt+=. Excel outlines the range it will add. On a Mac, use the AutoSum button on the Home tab.
Click B9 and press Alt+=, check the outlined range B2:B8, then press Enter. B9 shows 955. On a Mac, click the AutoSum button instead.
steps.explanation: AutoSum guesses the numbers above the cell. Enter accepts the suggestion, and B9 becomes =SUM(B2:B8).

common_mistakes.message: The formula is waiting for Enter. Press Enter to accept it.
That typed number will not update. Use AutoSum so B9 holds a formula.

steps.prompt: Three branches' sales sit in A2:C6, and row 7 under them is empty. Select A2:C7 and total all three columns with one AutoSum.
hints: Select the data and the empty row beneath it. One AutoSum then fills every column.
Select A2:C7, the data plus the empty bottom row. Pressing Alt+= writes a SUM under each column at once, with no need to press Enter.
Press Shift+Right twice and Shift+Down five times to select A2:C7, then press Alt+=. A7, B7 and C7 fill with the column totals.
steps.explanation: With several columns selected and an empty row below, AutoSum writes a total under every column in one go.

common_mistakes.message: Only one column was totalled. Select all three columns before pressing Alt+=.
Nothing has been totalled yet. Press Alt+= with the block selected.

steps.prompt: Three products' monthly sales are in B2:D4 and column E is empty. Select B2:E4 and total every row at once.
hints: Row totals need an empty column beside the data. Include it in your selection.
Select the figures plus the empty column on the right, B2:E4. AutoSum then writes a total at the end of every row.
Press Shift+Right three times and Shift+Down twice to select B2:E4, then press Alt+=. E2, E3 and E4 show 405, 295 and 215.
steps.explanation: When an empty column sits beside the selected data, AutoSum fills a total at the end of each row.

common_mistakes.message: Only the first row was totalled. Select B2:E4 so all three rows are included.
Nothing has been totalled yet. Press Alt+= with the block selected.

steps.prompt: Six exam scores are in B2:B7 and B8 is empty. You are in B8. Use the AutoSum arrow to show the class average, not the total.
hints: AutoSum is not only for totals. Where is the list of other functions?
The AutoSum button on the Home tab has a small arrow. Its list offers Sum, Average, Count Numbers, Max and Min. Click the empty cell under the scores first.
Click B8, open the AutoSum arrow, choose Average, check the range B2:B7, and press Enter. B8 shows 80.
steps.explanation: The AutoSum arrow offers Average, Count Numbers, Max and Min as well as Sum. Each writes the matching function.

common_mistakes.message: That is the total. Open the AutoSum arrow and choose Average.
The formula is waiting for Enter. Press Enter to accept it.

steps.prompt: A sales table has Q1 and Q2 in B2:C5, an empty Total column D and an empty Total row 6. Select B2:D6 and fill every row total, column total and the grand total with one AutoSum.
hints: Include both the empty row and the empty column in your selection.
Select B2:D6: the figures plus the empty Total column and the empty Total row. One Alt+= fills the row totals, the column totals and the grand total together.
Press Shift+Right twice and Shift+Down four times to select B2:D6, then press Alt+=. All seven totals appear, including the grand total, 2350.
steps.explanation: Selecting the data plus the empty total row and column lets one AutoSum fill every total, including the grand total in the corner.

common_mistakes.message: Row totals are missing. Include the empty Total column D in the selection.
The column totals are missing. Include the empty Total row 6 in the selection.

title: SUM Functions Skill Summary
objectives: By the end you can choose the right way to total a list, whatever layout it comes in.
about: This lesson brings together SUM, ranges, row and column totals, AutoSum, and separate cells. There is no new material, only practice. Real lists are rarely tidy, so you pick the version of SUM that fits each sheet. Look at the layout first. Is the list in one block, in two blocks, across a row, or scattered? Then choose the range and write the formula. Use AutoSum when the layout is simple, and type SUM when you need control. Always compare the total with a quick mental estimate, so a wrong range stands out at once.
syntax: SUM(range) · SUM(range1, range2) · SUM(cell, cell, cell) · AutoSum (Alt+=)

examples.scenario: A shop owner totals one block.
examples.why: One range gives one total.

examples.scenario: A clerk adds a typed amount to a range.
examples.why: A range and a number can sit in the same SUM.

examples.scenario: A manager adds only chosen days.
examples.why: Separate cells are listed with commas.

watch_out: Look at the layout first: one block, two blocks, a row, or scattered cells.
Check that no subtotal sits inside the range you add.
AutoSum is quickest for simple tables. Type SUM when you need to skip cells.
recap: You can now total any layout with confidence. Next, COUNT tells you how many entries a list holds.

steps.prompt: A car park's income for Monday to Friday is in B2:B6. Work out the weekly income in B7.
hints: One range, one total. Which function adds a list of numbers?
SUM(range) adds every number in the range. B2:B6 runs from Monday to Friday. Use the range instead of adding each cell by hand.
Type =SUM(B2:B6) in B7 and press Enter. The five days add up to 500.
steps.explanation: SUM adds the whole range B2:B6 in one step.

common_mistakes.message: Friday is missing. The range must reach B6.
That adds only Monday and Friday. Use SUM with the whole range.
Friday was counted twice. SUM already includes B6.

steps.prompt: Each rep's three quarters are in B2:D2. Work out Amina's year total in E2, ready to fill down to E4.
hints: The figures run across a row. Which range covers Q1 to Q3?
A range across a row looks like B2:D2. SUM adds all three quarters. Fill down and each rep gets their own total.
Type =SUM(B2:D2) in E2 and press Enter, then fill down to E4. Each rep's three quarters are added.
steps.explanation: A row range adds across. Filling down moves it to each rep's row.

common_mistakes.message: That adds Q1 for all three reps. Add across the row instead.
Q3 is missing. The range must reach column D.
That shows Q3 only. Add all three quarters.

steps.prompt: Four weeks of figures for Mon, Tue and Wed are in A2:C5, with row 6 empty. Total all three columns at once with AutoSum.
hints: Select the data plus the empty row below. One AutoSum covers every column.
Select A2:C6, the figures and the empty row 6, then press Alt+=. A total appears under each column. On a Mac, use the AutoSum button.
Press Shift+Right twice and Shift+Down four times to select A2:C6, then press Alt+=. A6, B6 and C6 show 42, 44 and 47.
steps.explanation: AutoSum totals every column of the selection that has an empty cell below its numbers.

common_mistakes.message: Only one column was totalled. Select all three columns first.
Nothing has been totalled yet. Press Alt+= with the block selected.

steps.prompt: Five monthly expenses are in B2:B6. A one-off payment of 250 is not in the table. In B8, work out the total including the one-off payment.
hints: SUM can take a range and a plain number together. How would you write both?
SUM accepts several arguments separated by commas. One can be a range and another a typed number, so the one-off payment can sit inside the brackets.
Type =SUM(B2:B6,250) in B8 and press Enter. The five expenses add to 250, and the one-off payment of 250 brings the total to 500.
steps.explanation: Each argument in SUM is added, whether it is a range or a typed number.

common_mistakes.message: The one-off payment is missing. Add 250 as a second argument.
That adds only two expenses. Use SUM with the whole range.
Multiplying gives a meaningless 62500. Add the payment.

steps.prompt: Only the Monday, Wednesday and Friday takings (B2, B4 and B6) go into this report. In D2, add just those three days.
hints: The days you want are not next to each other. How can SUM take separate cells?
SUM accepts single cells separated by commas. List only the cells you want, and it skips the days in between.
Type =SUM(B2,B4,B6) in D2 and press Enter. It adds Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and ignores Tuesday and Thursday. The answer is 450.
steps.explanation: Listing single cells in SUM adds only those cells.

common_mistakes.message: That adds all five days. List only B2, B4 and B6.
Friday is missing. Add B6 too.
That is a block of three days, including Tuesday. List the separate cells.

title: COUNT Function
objectives: By the end you can count how many cells hold numbers, dates or valid results, and explain what COUNT skips.
about: COUNT tells you how many cells in a range contain numbers. It does not add the numbers up. It only counts them. Dates and times count as numbers too, because Excel stores them as numbers. Text, blank cells, and error values are ignored. Use COUNT to see how many sales were made. Use it to count students who sat a test, or entries that are filled in. To use it, type =COUNT(, select the range, close the bracket, and press Enter. You can give it several ranges separated by commas.

examples.scenario: A stall owner counts the days that have takings.
examples.why: The blank day is skipped.

examples.scenario: A teacher counts who sat a test.
examples.why: The text absent is not a number.

examples.scenario: A clerk counts entries in two lists.
examples.why: Several ranges are searched and the counts are combined.

examples.scenario: A courier counts delivered orders by their dates.
examples.why: A date is a number, so it is counted.

watch_out: COUNT counts numbers only. A cell with text, even a number typed as text, is skipped.
A blank cell and a zero are different. Zero is a number and counts. A blank does not.
To count text or every filled cell, use COUNTA, which you meet in lesson 30.
recap: You can now count how many numeric entries a list holds. Next, you will practise COUNT in realistic situations.

steps.prompt: The stall's takings for the week are in B2:B8, but two days have no entry yet. In D2, count how many days have takings.
hints: You want how many days have a number, not their total. Which function counts numbers?
COUNT(range) counts the cells that contain numbers and skips blanks and text. It tells you how many entries exist, while SUM adds their values.
Type =COUNT(B2:B8) in D2 and press Enter. Five days have takings, so the answer is 5.
steps.explanation: COUNT counts cells that hold numbers. The two empty days are skipped.

common_mistakes.message: SUM adds the takings, 595. COUNT tells you how many days have takings.
The range stops at Friday. Saturday and Sunday are in B7 and B8.
Column A holds day names, which are text. COUNT counts numbers.

steps.prompt: A class register lists test scores in B2:B9. Two students are marked absent in text. In D2, count how many students actually sat the test.
hints: The word absent is text, not a score. Which function counts only the numbers?
COUNT counts numbers and ignores text, so the cells that say absent are not counted. Give it the whole score range.
Type =COUNT(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. Six cells hold scores and two hold text, so the answer is 6.
steps.explanation: COUNT skips text, so only the six real scores are counted.

common_mistakes.message: COUNTA counts every filled cell, including the text absent, giving 8. COUNT counts only numbers.
SUM adds the scores. COUNT tells you how many there are.
The range stops one row early. The last student is in row 9.

steps.prompt: Two classes' scores are in B2:B5 and D2:D5, with some entries still blank. In F2, count all the scores that have been entered.
hints: There are two separate lists. How can COUNT look at both?
COUNT accepts several ranges separated by commas, and adds up the numbers found in each. Give it the Class A range and the Class B range.
Type =COUNT(B2:B5,D2:D5) in F2 and press Enter. Class A has 3 scores and Class B has 2, so the answer is 5.
steps.explanation: Each range given to COUNT is searched, and the counts are combined.

common_mistakes.message: That counts Class A only. Add the Class B range.
That counts Class B only. Add the Class A range.
SUM adds the scores. COUNT tells you how many there are.

steps.prompt: Delivery dates are in B2:B7, and two orders have not been delivered yet, so their cells are blank. In D2, count how many orders have a delivery date.
hints: Excel stores dates as numbers. Which function counts cells that hold numbers?
A date is a number to Excel, so COUNT counts it. Blank cells are skipped. Give COUNT the whole delivery column.
Type =COUNT(B2:B7) in D2 and press Enter. Four orders have a date, so the answer is 4.
steps.explanation: Dates are stored as numbers, so COUNT counts every cell that holds a date.

common_mistakes.message: SUM adds the date numbers into a huge meaningless value. COUNT tells you how many dates there are.
The range stops at ORD-4. ORD-5 and ORD-6 are in rows 6 and 7.
Column A holds order codes, which are text. COUNT counts numbers.

steps.prompt: A price list shows #DIV/0! errors in two rows because of a broken calculation. In D2, count how many rows hold a valid price.
hints: Errors are not numbers. Which function counts only valid numbers?
COUNT counts only cells that hold numbers. Error values, text and blanks are all skipped. COUNTA would count the errors as filled cells.
Type =COUNT(B2:B7) in D2 and press Enter. Four rows hold valid prices, and the two errors are ignored. The answer is 4.
steps.explanation: COUNT ignores error values, so only the four valid prices are counted.

common_mistakes.message: COUNTA counts every filled cell, including the two error cells, giving 6. COUNT counts only valid numbers.
The range stops at Lamp. The list runs to row 7.
SUM shows #DIV/0! because of the errors. COUNT ignores them.

title: COUNT Practice
objectives: By the end you can use COUNT in everyday situations: counting paid items, counting across blocks, comparing lists and building sentences.
about: This is a practice lesson, so there is no new material. You will use COUNT where it earns its place. You will count paid invoices, filled cells, the gap between two lists, and entries inside a sentence. You will also combine it with SUM to find an average by hand. That prepares you for AVERAGE. For each problem, decide what you are counting before you type. Ask whether the cells hold numbers, text, or blanks, because COUNT only counts numbers. Then choose the range that covers every cell you care about.

examples.scenario: An office counts paid invoices.
examples.why: A blank means unpaid, so only paid invoices are counted.

examples.scenario: A manager finds an average by hand.
examples.why: The total is 200 and two orders have amounts.

examples.scenario: A clerk builds a progress message.
examples.why: COUNT supplies the number and & joins the words.

watch_out: Decide what you are counting before you type: numbers, text or blanks.
Use the same range in SUM and COUNT when you build an average by hand.
recap: You can now apply COUNT to realistic problems. Next, a summary lesson mixes COUNT with SUM and AutoSum.

steps.prompt: An invoice list shows the paid amount in column B. Unpaid invoices are blank. In D2, count how many invoices have been paid.
hints: Paid invoices have a number in column B, unpaid ones are blank. Which function counts numbers?
COUNT counts the cells that hold numbers and skips blanks. Each paid invoice has an amount, so counting the amounts counts the paid invoices.
Type =COUNT(B2:B8) in D2 and press Enter. Four invoices have an amount, so the answer is 4.
steps.explanation: Each paid invoice has an amount, so counting the amounts counts the paid invoices.

common_mistakes.message: SUM adds the amounts, 1430. COUNT tells you how many were paid.
The range stops at INV-4. The list runs to row 8.
Column A holds invoice codes, which are text. COUNT counts numbers.

steps.prompt: A sales table has Q1 and Q2 figures in B2:C5, with a few gaps. In E2, count how many figures have been entered in total.
hints: The figures sit in two columns. How can one range cover both?
A range can cover several columns at once. B2:C5 is a block of two columns and four rows, and COUNT counts every number inside it.
Type =COUNT(B2:C5) in E2 and press Enter. The block holds 6 numbers and 2 gaps, so the answer is 6.
steps.explanation: A rectangular range such as B2:C5 is counted cell by cell, so gaps are skipped.

common_mistakes.message: That counts Q1 only, 3. Include column C as well.
The block stops at Tape. Glue is in row 5.
SUM adds the figures, 165. COUNT tells you how many were entered.

steps.prompt: Orders are in B2:B7 and one order has no amount yet. In D2, work out the average order size: the total of the amounts divided by how many amounts there are.
hints: An average is a total divided by a count. Which two functions give those?
Divide the SUM of the amounts by the COUNT of the amounts. COUNT skips the blank order, so it divides by 5, not 6.
Type =SUM(B2:B7)/COUNT(B2:B7) in D2 and press Enter. The total is 600, divided by 5 amounts, so the average order is 120.
steps.explanation: SUM gives the total, 600, and COUNT gives the number of amounts, 5. Dividing gives 120.

common_mistakes.message: That divides by 6, but only 5 orders have an amount. Use COUNT.
The COUNT range stops one row early. Use the same range in both.
That divides the wrong way round. Divide the total by the count.

steps.prompt: Class A's scores are in B2:B6 and Class B's are in D2:D6. In F2, work out how many more scores Class A has entered than Class B.
hints: You need two counts and the gap between them. How do you combine them?
Count each class separately, then subtract. Put Class A's count first so the answer is how many more Class A has.
Type =COUNT(B2:B6)-COUNT(D2:D6) in F2 and press Enter. Class A has 4 scores and Class B has 2, so the difference is 2.
steps.explanation: Two COUNT results can be combined with an operator, just like any other numbers.

common_mistakes.message: That subtracts the wrong way round and gives -2. Class A comes first.
That counts every score in both classes, 6. You need the difference.
That adds the two counts, 6. You need how many more Class A has.

steps.prompt: A timesheet has hours for five days in B2:B6, and one day is still blank. In D2, show a sentence such as 4 of 5 days recorded, built from the count of recorded days.
hints: You need a number and some words in one cell. Which symbol joins them?
The & symbol joins text. COUNT gives the number, and the words go in quotation marks, starting with a space so the pieces do not run together.
Type =COUNT(B2:B6)&" of 5 days recorded" in D2 and press Enter. The result is 4 of 5 days recorded.
steps.explanation: COUNT gives the number, and & joins it to the text. The sentence updates as days are filled in.

common_mistakes.message: That shows only the number, 4. Join it to the words with &.
The words ran into the number. Start the text with a space.
That typed sentence will not update. Build it from COUNT.

title: COUNT Skill Summary
objectives: By the end you can count numbers confidently across ranges, blocks and messy data, and combine COUNT with SUM.
about: This lesson mixes everything you have learned about COUNT, with no new material. You will count ratings with gaps and use the AutoSum list for Count Numbers. You will count across a block that holds text. You will divide a total by a count, and count valid results among errors. The skill that matters is knowing what COUNT counts. It counts numbers, including dates, and it skips text, blanks, and errors. Read each problem and ask what the cells hold before you pick a range. A quick check against the visible data catches most mistakes.
syntax: COUNT(range) · COUNT(range1, range2) · SUM(range)/COUNT(range) · AutoSum > Count Numbers

examples.scenario: A researcher counts survey answers.
examples.why: The blank is skipped.

examples.scenario: A payroll clerk counts days worked with the AutoSum list.
examples.why: The list writes a COUNT formula for you.

examples.scenario: An analyst counts valid results among errors.
examples.why: Errors are ignored by COUNT.

watch_out: Ask what the cells hold: numbers, text, blanks or errors.
COUNT and COUNTA answer different questions. COUNT counts numbers, COUNTA counts everything filled.
recap: You can now count numbers in any layout. Next, COUNTA and COUNTBLANK count text and empty cells.

steps.prompt: A survey sheet lists customer ratings in B2:B8, and two customers did not answer. In D2, count how many ratings were given.
hints: Ratings are numbers and blanks mean no answer. Which function counts numbers?
COUNT counts the cells that hold numbers and skips the blanks. Give it the whole rating range.
Type =COUNT(B2:B8) in D2 and press Enter. Five customers gave a rating.
steps.explanation: COUNT counts the five cells that hold ratings and skips the two blanks.

common_mistakes.message: SUM adds the ratings, 21. COUNT tells you how many there are.
The range stops at C4. The list runs to row 8.
Column A holds customer codes, which are text. COUNT counts numbers.

steps.prompt: Five days of hours are in B2:B6 and B7 is empty. You are in B7. Use the AutoSum arrow to count how many days have hours.
hints: AutoSum can count as well as add. Where do you choose Count Numbers?
The AutoSum button on the Home tab has a small arrow. Choose Count Numbers from its list, check the outlined range, and press Enter.
Click B7, open the AutoSum arrow, choose Count Numbers, check B2:B6, and press Enter. B7 shows 5.
steps.explanation: Count Numbers in the AutoSum list writes a COUNT formula for the numbers above the cell.

common_mistakes.message: The formula is waiting for Enter. Press Enter to accept it.
That is the total hours. Open the AutoSum arrow and choose Count Numbers.

steps.prompt: Orders have Q1 amounts in B2:B6 and Q2 amounts in C2:C6. Some cells say n/a and some are blank. In E2, count how many real amounts there are.
hints: Text and blanks are not amounts. Which function counts only numbers across a block?
COUNT counts numbers in any range, including a block of several columns. Text such as n/a and blank cells are skipped.
Type =COUNT(B2:C6) in E2 and press Enter. Seven cells hold real amounts, so the answer is 7.
steps.explanation: COUNT over the whole block skips the n/a text and the blank, leaving the seven real amounts.

common_mistakes.message: COUNTA counts every filled cell, including n/a, giving 9. COUNT counts only numbers.
That counts Q1 only, 4. Include column C.
SUM adds the amounts. COUNT tells you how many there are.

steps.prompt: Hours worked Monday to Friday are in B2:B6, and Wednesday was a day off, so it is blank. In D2, work out the average hours per day actually worked.
hints: An average per day worked divides the total hours by the days worked. Which functions give those?
Divide SUM of the hours by COUNT of the hours. COUNT skips the blank day off, so only days worked are counted.
Type =SUM(B2:B6)/COUNT(B2:B6) in D2 and press Enter. The total is 28 hours over 4 days worked, so the average is 7.
steps.explanation: COUNT skips the blank day off, so the total divides by 4 days worked, not 5.

common_mistakes.message: That divides by 5, but only 4 days were worked. Use COUNT.
The COUNT range stops early. Use the same range in both.
That divides the wrong way round. Divide the total by the count.

steps.prompt: A store report shows #DIV/0! errors in two rows. In D2, count how many stores have a valid result.
hints: Errors are not numbers. Which function counts only valid numbers?
COUNT counts only cells that hold numbers. Error values, text and blanks are skipped. COUNTA would count the errors as filled cells.
Type =COUNT(B2:B7) in D2 and press Enter. Four stores have a valid result, and the two errors are ignored.
steps.explanation: COUNT ignores error values, so only the four valid results are counted.

common_mistakes.message: COUNTA counts every filled cell, including the two errors, giving 6. COUNT counts only valid numbers.
The range stops at Truro. The list runs to row 7.
SUM shows #DIV/0! because of the errors. COUNT ignores them.

title: Other Count Functions
objectives: By the end you can count filled cells with COUNTA, empty cells with COUNTBLANK, and text entries by combining them with COUNT.
about: COUNT only counts numbers, so Excel has two more counting functions. COUNTA counts every cell that is not empty, including text, numbers and errors. COUNTBLANK counts the cells that are empty. Use COUNTA to count customers, orders or names, and COUNTBLANK to find missing data. Together with COUNT they answer how many entries exist, how many are missing, and how many are text. Subtract COUNT from COUNTA to count only the text. To use them, type the name, select the range, and press Enter. Conditional counting with COUNTIF comes later, in lesson 85.

examples.scenario: A manager counts how many customers are on a list.
examples.why: COUNTA counts text, and the gap is skipped.

examples.scenario: An office checks for missing phone numbers.
examples.why: COUNTBLANK counts the empty cells.

examples.scenario: A teacher counts absent students recorded as text.
examples.why: Filled cells minus numbers leaves the text.

examples.scenario: An analyst counts a growing list, minus its heading.
examples.why: The whole column grows with the list.

watch_out: COUNTA counts errors and cells that look empty but hold a space or an empty text result.
COUNTBLANK counts cells that look empty, including cells with an empty text result.
A whole-column range includes the heading, so subtract 1 when the heading is text.
recap: You can now count any kind of entry or gap. Next, you will move on from counting to the AVERAGE function.

steps.prompt: A customer list in A2:A9 has a few empty rows between the names. In D2, count how many customers are listed.
hints: Names are text, so COUNT will not count them. Which function counts every filled cell?
COUNTA counts every cell that is not empty, whether it holds text, numbers or errors. COUNT counts only numbers. For a list of names, COUNTA is the right tool.
Type =COUNTA(A2:A9) in D2 and press Enter. Six of the eight cells hold a name, so the answer is 6.
steps.explanation: COUNTA counts every non-empty cell, so text such as names is included.

common_mistakes.message: COUNT counts only numbers, so names give 0. Use COUNTA.
That includes the heading in A1, giving 7. Start at A2.
COUNTBLANK counts the empty rows, 2. COUNTA counts the filled ones.

steps.prompt: Phone numbers are in B2:B9, and some customers have none. In D2, count how many customers are missing a phone number.
hints: You want to count the gaps, not the filled cells. Which function counts empty cells?
COUNTBLANK counts the cells in a range that are empty. It is the opposite of COUNTA, so it shows what is missing.
Type =COUNTBLANK(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. Three phone cells are empty, so the answer is 3.
steps.explanation: COUNTBLANK counts empty cells, which makes missing data easy to measure.

common_mistakes.message: COUNTA counts the filled phone numbers, 5. COUNTBLANK counts the gaps.
The phone numbers are text, so COUNT gives 0. Use COUNTBLANK.
The range stops at Tomas. The list runs to row 9.

steps.prompt: Scores are in B2:B9 and some students are marked absent in text. In D2, work out how many text entries there are, without counting the numbers.
hints: Every filled cell minus the numbers leaves the text. Which two functions give those?
COUNTA counts every filled cell and COUNT counts only the numbers. Subtract COUNT from COUNTA and what is left is the text entries.
Type =COUNTA(B2:B9)-COUNT(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. 8 filled cells minus 6 numbers leaves 2 text entries.
steps.explanation: COUNTA minus COUNT leaves the cells that are filled but not numeric, which here are the absent students.

common_mistakes.message: That counts every filled cell, 8. Subtract the numbers.
That counts the scores, 6. You want the text entries.
There are no empty cells here. Subtract COUNT from COUNTA instead.

steps.prompt: Survey answers are in B2:B9, and some customers have not answered. In D2, show what share of customers have answered, as a percentage.
hints: A share is the answered count divided by the total customers. Which functions give those?
Answered cells are counted with COUNTA. The total is answered plus empty cells, with COUNTBLANK counting the empty ones. Divide answered by total.
Type =COUNTA(B2:B9)/(COUNTA(B2:B9)+COUNTBLANK(B2:B9)) in D2 and press Enter. 5 of 8 customers answered, which is 62.5%.
steps.explanation: COUNTA gives the answered cells, and COUNTA plus COUNTBLANK gives every row, so dividing gives the share.

common_mistakes.message: That is the number answered, 5, not a share. Divide it by the total.
That divides the unanswered by the answered, 0.6. Divide answered by the total.
COUNT gives 0 because answers are text, and 8 is typed in. Use COUNTA.

steps.prompt: Column A lists orders under a heading in A1, and new orders will be added below. In D2, count the orders using the whole column so new ones are included automatically.
hints: The whole column includes the heading too. How do you avoid counting it?
A whole-column range such as A:A grows with the list. COUNTA counts the heading as well, so subtract 1 for the heading.
Type =COUNTA(A:A)-1 in D2 and press Enter. The column holds 8 filled cells including the heading, so 7 orders.
steps.explanation: A:A covers the whole column, so new orders are counted. Subtracting 1 removes the heading.

common_mistakes.message: That includes the heading in A1, giving 8. Subtract 1.
That range stops at row 8, so new orders will be missed. Use the whole column.
Order codes are text, so COUNT gives 0. Use COUNTA.

title: AVERAGE Function
objectives: By the end you can find averages of lists, rows and several ranges, and explain how AVERAGE treats blanks, text and zeros.
about: An average tells you the typical value in a list. Excel adds up the numbers and divides by how many there are. AVERAGE does both steps for you. This is also called the mean. Give it a range, several ranges, or single cells. It ignores blank cells and text, so a note such as n/a does not spoil the result. A zero is a real number and does count. Use AVERAGE for scores, sales per day, ratings, and costs. To use it, type =AVERAGE(, select the cells, close the bracket, and press Enter.

examples.scenario: A teacher averages exam scores.
examples.why: The total is 240 and there are 3 scores.

examples.scenario: A researcher averages ratings that include n/a.
examples.why: The text is skipped, so only two ratings count.

examples.scenario: A shop owner averages sales that include a zero day.
examples.why: The zero counts, so the average is 18 divided by 3.

examples.scenario: A manager averages three months for one product.
examples.why: A row range works the same way.

watch_out: AVERAGE ignores blanks and text but counts zeros. A zero day pulls the average down.
If a range holds no numbers at all, AVERAGE shows #DIV/0!.
One very large or very small value can drag the average. Lesson 34 shows MEDIAN, which resists that.
recap: You can now find the typical value of any list. Next, MIN, MAX, LARGE and SMALL find the extremes.

steps.prompt: Six exam scores are in B2:B7. In B8, work out the class average.
hints: An average is the typical value of a list. Which function finds it?
AVERAGE(range) adds the numbers in the range and divides by how many there are. Give it the whole list of scores.
Type =AVERAGE(B2:B7) in B8 and press Enter. The six scores add to 480, and 480 divided by 6 is 80.
steps.explanation: AVERAGE adds the scores and divides by how many there are.

common_mistakes.message: SUM gives the total, 480. AVERAGE divides it by the number of scores.
The range stops at Leila. Omar's score is in B7.
That divides by 7, but there are 6 scores. Use AVERAGE.

steps.prompt: Customer ratings are in B2:B8, and two customers wrote n/a. In B9, work out the average rating from the real ratings only.
hints: The text n/a is not a rating. How does AVERAGE treat text in a range?
AVERAGE ignores text and blank cells, so n/a is left out of both the total and the count. Give it the whole range.
Type =AVERAGE(B2:B8) in B9 and press Enter. Five real ratings add to 21, and 21 divided by 5 is 4.2.
steps.explanation: AVERAGE skips the n/a text, so it divides by 5 real ratings and not by 7 cells.

common_mistakes.message: That divides by all 7 cells, including n/a. AVERAGE counts only real ratings.
COUNTA counts the n/a text as well, giving 3. Use AVERAGE or COUNT.
That typed 5 will not follow the data. Use AVERAGE.

steps.prompt: Units sold Monday to Sunday are in B2:B8. Thursday sold 0, and Saturday has not been entered yet. In D2, work out the average units per recorded day.
hints: A zero is a real day. A blank is no entry. Which one does AVERAGE count?
AVERAGE counts a zero as a number, so Thursday pulls the average down. It skips the blank Saturday completely. Give it the whole range.
Type =AVERAGE(B2:B8) in D2 and press Enter. The six recorded days add to 60, and 60 divided by 6 is 10.
steps.explanation: Zero is a value and counts. A blank is skipped. That is why the average is 10 and not 8.57.

common_mistakes.message: That divides by 7, but Saturday is not recorded. AVERAGE skips the blank.
That skips Thursday's zero. A zero is a real day and must count.
The COUNT range stops early. Use AVERAGE with the whole range.

steps.prompt: Two shifts' sales are in B2:B5 and D2:D5. In F2, work out the overall average across both shifts.
hints: There are two lists, and every sale counts equally. How can AVERAGE take both?
AVERAGE accepts several ranges separated by commas, and averages every number in them together. Do not average the two averages.
Type =AVERAGE(B2:B5,D2:D5) in F2 and press Enter. The eight sales add to 800, and 800 divided by 8 is 100.
steps.explanation: AVERAGE with two ranges treats all eight sales as one list.

common_mistakes.message: That adds the two averages, 200. Average all the sales together.
That averages Shift A only. Add Shift B as a second range.
That divides by 4, but there are 8 sales. Use AVERAGE.

steps.prompt: Each product's January, February and March sales are in B2:D2. In E2, work out Widget's average month, ready to fill down to E5.
hints: The figures run across a row. Which range covers January to March?
AVERAGE works on a row range such as B2:D2. Fill the formula down and each product averages its own three months.
Type =AVERAGE(B2:D2) in E2 and press Enter, then fill down to E5. Widget's three months average 135.
steps.explanation: AVERAGE over a row range averages that product's months, and filling down repeats it for each row.

common_mistakes.message: Without brackets only March is divided by 3. Use AVERAGE, or add brackets.
That averages the January column. Average across the row.
That divides by 4, but there are 3 months. Use AVERAGE.

title: MIN, MAX, LARGE, SMALL Functions
objectives: By the end you can find the highest, lowest, n-th highest and n-th lowest values, and combine several at once with curly brackets.
about: MAX and MIN find the largest and smallest numbers in a range. LARGE and SMALL go further. They return the second largest, the third smallest, or any position you choose. You give them the range and the position, k. Use them to find the best sale, the fastest time, the runner-up, or the cheapest few prices. Put several positions in curly brackets, such as {1,2,3}, to get the top three together. Wrap the result in AVERAGE or SUM to combine them. All four functions ignore text and blank cells. They work on rows as well as columns.
syntax: MIN(range) · MAX(range) · LARGE(range, k) · SMALL(range, k) · LARGE(range, {1,2,3})

examples.scenario: A manager finds the best sale.
examples.why: MAX returns the largest number.

examples.scenario: A coach finds the fastest runner.
examples.why: MIN returns the smallest number.

examples.scenario: A teacher finds the runner-up score.
examples.why: k = 2 gives the second largest.

examples.scenario: An analyst averages the top three sales.
examples.why: The curly brackets ask for three positions at once.

watch_out: k must be between 1 and the number of values, or you get #NUM!.
LARGE(range,1) is the same as MAX, and SMALL(range,1) is the same as MIN.
Curly brackets such as {1,2,3} ask for several positions at once. Wrap LARGE in AVERAGE or SUM to combine them.
recap: You can now find the extremes of any list. Next, a practice lesson applies these functions to real problems.

steps.prompt: Six reps' sales are in B2:B7. In D2, show the best single sale.
hints: You want the biggest value in a list. Which function finds it?
MAX(range) returns the largest number in the range. Give it the whole list, and it picks the biggest.
Type =MAX(B2:B7) in D2 and press Enter. The biggest of the six sales is 510.
steps.explanation: MAX scans the range and returns the largest number.

common_mistakes.message: MIN returns the smallest, 295. MAX returns the biggest.
That returns the second largest, 460. MAX returns the biggest.
SUM adds all the sales. MAX picks the biggest one.

steps.prompt: Six runners' times in seconds are in B2:B7. In D2, show the fastest time.
hints: The fastest runner has the smallest time. Which function finds the smallest value?
MIN(range) returns the smallest number in the range. For race times, the smallest time is the fastest.
Type =MIN(B2:B7) in D2 and press Enter. The smallest of the six times is 49.8 seconds.
steps.explanation: MIN scans the range and returns the smallest number.

common_mistakes.message: MAX returns the slowest time, 53.1. MIN returns the fastest.
That returns the second smallest, 49.9. MIN returns the smallest.
AVERAGE gives the typical time. MIN gives the fastest.

steps.prompt: Six students' scores are in B2:B7. In D2, show the second highest score, to award the runner-up prize.
hints: MAX only gives the top value. Which function can give the second, third, or fourth?
LARGE(range, k) returns the k-th largest number. With k set to 2 it gives the second largest. SMALL works the same way from the bottom.
Type =LARGE(B2:B7,2) in D2 and press Enter. The top score is 95, and the second highest is 92.
steps.explanation: LARGE takes a position, k. k = 1 is the biggest, k = 2 is the second biggest, and so on.

common_mistakes.message: MAX returns the highest score, 95. You need the second highest.
SMALL counts from the bottom. Use LARGE to count from the top.
k = 3 gives the third highest, 90. Use k = 2.

steps.prompt: Six suppliers' prices are in B2:B7. In D2, show the third cheapest price.
hints: Cheapest means smallest. Which function can give the third smallest?
SMALL(range, k) returns the k-th smallest number. With k set to 3 it gives the third cheapest price.
Type =SMALL(B2:B7,3) in D2 and press Enter. The prices in order are 7.2, 8, then 9.5, so the third cheapest is 9.5.
steps.explanation: SMALL counts from the bottom. k = 3 gives the third smallest.

common_mistakes.message: LARGE counts from the top, giving 11. Use SMALL for the cheapest.
MIN gives the cheapest, 7.2. You need the third cheapest.
k = 2 gives the second cheapest, 8. Use k = 3.

steps.prompt: Eight reps' sales are in B2:B9. In D2, work out the average of the three highest sales.
hints: You need the three biggest values together. How can LARGE return several positions at once?
Put the positions in curly brackets, {1,2,3}, as the second part of LARGE. It then returns the first, second and third largest together, and AVERAGE averages them.
Type =AVERAGE(LARGE(B2:B9,{1,2,3})) in D2 and press Enter. The top three are 520, 500 and 480, and their average is 500.
steps.explanation: The curly brackets ask LARGE for three positions at once. AVERAGE then averages those three values.

common_mistakes.message: That averages only the third largest, 480. Use {1,2,3} for the top three.
SUM adds the top three, 1500. AVERAGE finds their average.
That divides the third largest by 3. Average the top three values.
MAX gives only the biggest sale, 520. You need the top three averaged.

title: MIN, MAX, LARGE, SMALL Practice
objectives: By the end you can combine MIN, MAX, LARGE and SMALL with each other and with arithmetic to answer real questions.
about: This is a practice lesson, so there is no new material. You will use MIN, MAX, LARGE and SMALL on real questions. You will find the spread of a list and a bonus for the top performer. You will find the gap to the runner-up and the cost of the two cheapest options. You will also average the fastest times. Most questions need two steps. First find the extremes, then calculate with them. Decide which positions you need before you type, such as the first, the second, or the top three. Use curly brackets when you need several positions at once.

examples.scenario: A weather office finds the spread of temperatures.
examples.why: Highest minus lowest is the spread.

examples.scenario: A manager finds the gap between first and second place.
examples.why: MAX gives first place and LARGE with k = 2 gives second.

examples.scenario: A coach averages the two fastest times.
examples.why: The curly brackets return two positions at once.

watch_out: Work out which positions you need first: the first, the second, or the top few.
Both MAX and LARGE ignore text and blanks, so tidy-looking gaps are safe.
recap: You can now answer extreme-value questions. Next, MEDIAN finds the middle value of a list.

steps.prompt: Daily temperatures are in B2:B7. In D2, work out the spread: the highest temperature minus the lowest.
hints: The spread is the gap between the highest and the lowest. Which two functions give those?
Subtract MIN from MAX. Both take the same range, so the result is the distance between the two extremes.
Type =MAX(B2:B7)-MIN(B2:B7) in D2 and press Enter. The highest is 25 and the lowest is 12, so the spread is 13.
steps.explanation: MAX minus MIN gives the distance between the highest and lowest values.

common_mistakes.message: That is the highest temperature, 25. Subtract the lowest.
That subtracts the wrong way round and gives -13. Highest first.
That adds them, 37. The spread is the difference.

steps.prompt: Six reps' sales are in B2:B7. The top performer earns a bonus of 10% of their sale. In D2, work out the bonus.
hints: The bonus depends on the biggest sale. Which function finds it, and how do you take 10%?
Find the largest sale with MAX, then multiply by 10%. You can type 10% or 0.1, and Excel treats them the same.
Type =MAX(B2:B7)*10% in D2 and press Enter. The top sale is 5100, and 10% of it is 510.
steps.explanation: MAX finds the top sale and multiplying by 10% gives the bonus.

common_mistakes.message: That takes 10% of the total, 2405. The bonus is on the top sale only.
That is the top sale, 5100. Take 10% of it.
MIN picks the lowest sale. The bonus is on the highest.

steps.prompt: Six students' scores are in B2:B7. In D2, work out the gap between the highest score and the second highest score.
hints: The gap is the difference between the best and the runner-up. Which functions find each?
The highest score is MAX, or LARGE with k = 1. The second highest is LARGE with k = 2. Subtract the second from the first.
Type =MAX(B2:B7)-LARGE(B2:B7,2) in D2 and press Enter. The highest is 95 and the second is 92, so the gap is 3.
steps.explanation: MAX gives the top score and LARGE with k = 2 gives the runner-up. Subtracting shows the gap.

common_mistakes.message: That is the gap to the lowest score, 16. You need the second highest.
That is the gap between the second and third, 2. Start from the highest.
That typed 92 will not update. Use LARGE.

steps.prompt: Six suppliers' prices are in B2:B7. In D2, work out the combined price of buying from the two cheapest suppliers.
hints: You need the smallest and the second smallest added together. Which function finds each?
SMALL with k = 1 is the cheapest and with k = 2 is the next cheapest. Add the two results together.
Type =SMALL(B2:B7,1)+SMALL(B2:B7,2) in D2 and press Enter. The two cheapest are 7.2 and 8, which add to 15.2.
steps.explanation: SMALL returns the cheapest two prices, and adding them gives their combined cost.

common_mistakes.message: That is only the second cheapest, 8. Add the cheapest too.
That doubles the cheapest, 14.4. Add the two cheapest prices.
That adds every price. You need only the two cheapest.

steps.prompt: Eight heats' times in seconds are in B2:B9. In D2, work out the average of the two fastest times.
hints: You need the two smallest times together. How can SMALL return two positions at once?
Put the positions in curly brackets, {1,2}, as the second part of SMALL. It returns the smallest and second smallest together, and AVERAGE averages them.
Type =AVERAGE(SMALL(B2:B9,{1,2})) in D2 and press Enter. The two fastest are 49.8 and 49.9, and their average is 49.85.
steps.explanation: The curly brackets ask SMALL for two positions. AVERAGE then averages the two fastest times.

common_mistakes.message: That averages only the second fastest, 49.9. Use {1,2} for both.
MIN gives only the fastest time, 49.8. You need two averaged.
That averages every heat. You need only the two fastest.

title: MEDIAN Function
objectives: By the end you can find the middle value of a list, and explain when the median describes data better than the average.
about: The median is the middle value of a list once the numbers are in order. Half the values are below it and half are above it. Unlike the average, it is not pulled around by one huge number. Excel's MEDIAN function finds it for you, without sorting the list. With an even number of values, it averages the two middle ones. Use MEDIAN when a few extreme values would distort the average, as with salaries, house prices, or delivery times. It ignores text and blank cells. To use it, type =MEDIAN(, select the cells, close the bracket, and press Enter.

examples.scenario: An HR officer finds the typical salary.
examples.why: With four values, MEDIAN averages the two middle ones, 2100 and 2250.

examples.scenario: A courier finds the middle delivery time.
examples.why: In order the times are 25, 30, 45, so the middle is 30.

examples.scenario: A researcher takes the median of ratings that include n/a.
examples.why: The text is skipped, so the middle of 2, 4, 5 is 4.

examples.scenario: An estate agent reports a typical house price.
examples.why: The 950 mansion does not move the median.

watch_out: The median and the average can be very different when one value is extreme.
MEDIAN ignores text and blank cells, but a zero is a number and counts.
With an even number of values the median is the average of the two middle ones, so it may not appear in the list.
recap: You can now find the middle of any list. Next, MODE finds the most common value.

steps.prompt: Five salaries are in B2:B6, and one is far higher than the rest. In D2, show the middle salary.
hints: The middle value sits in the centre when the list is in order. Which function finds it?
MEDIAN(range) returns the middle value once the numbers are in order. With five salaries it is the third one. You do not need to sort the list yourself.
Type =MEDIAN(B2:B6) in D2 and press Enter. In order the salaries are 1900, 2100, 2250, 2400, 8000, so the middle is 2250.
steps.explanation: MEDIAN sorts the numbers behind the scenes and returns the middle one.

common_mistakes.message: AVERAGE is pulled up by the 8000 and gives 3330. MEDIAN gives the middle value.
MAX returns the highest salary, 8000. MEDIAN returns the middle.
MIN returns the lowest salary, 1900. MEDIAN returns the middle.

steps.prompt: Six delivery times in minutes are in B2:B7, and one took very long. In D2, show the median delivery time.
hints: With an even number of values there is no single middle. What does MEDIAN do?
With six values, MEDIAN averages the two middle ones. In order they are 25, 30, 35, 45, 50, 90, so it averages 35 and 45.
Type =MEDIAN(B2:B7) in D2 and press Enter. The two middle values are 35 and 45, and their average is 40.
steps.explanation: With an even count, MEDIAN averages the two middle values.

common_mistakes.message: AVERAGE is pulled up by the 90 and gives 45.83. MEDIAN gives the middle.
MAX gives the longest time, 90. MEDIAN gives the middle.
The range stops one row early. The list runs to row 7.

steps.prompt: Customer ratings are in B2:B9, and some say n/a. In D2, show the median rating from the real ratings only.
hints: MEDIAN ignores text. Which ratings does it use here?
MEDIAN skips text and blank cells, so n/a is left out. Give it the whole range, and it works with the six real ratings.
Type =MEDIAN(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. The real ratings in order are 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, and the middle two are both 4.
steps.explanation: MEDIAN skips the n/a text and uses only the real ratings.

common_mistakes.message: AVERAGE gives 3.83. MEDIAN gives the middle rating.
MAX gives the top rating, 5. MEDIAN gives the middle.
MIN gives the lowest rating, 2. MEDIAN gives the middle.

steps.prompt: Five house prices (in thousands) are in B2:B6, and one mansion is far above the rest. In D2, show the typical price, one that the mansion does not distort.
hints: One extreme value drags the average. Which statistic resists that?
MEDIAN depends on the middle position, not on how large the extremes are. A single mansion cannot pull it far.
Type =MEDIAN(B2:B6) in D2 and press Enter. In order the prices are 180, 195, 205, 210, 950, and the middle is 205.
steps.explanation: The median ignores how extreme the highest price is, so it describes a typical house better here.

common_mistakes.message: AVERAGE is dragged up by the mansion to 348. Use MEDIAN.
MAX is the mansion's price, 950. Use MEDIAN.
MIN is the cheapest house, 180. Use MEDIAN.

steps.prompt: Two shops' daily takings are in B2:B5 and D2:D5. In F2, show the median of all eight days together.
hints: There are two lists, but the median is of all the days together. How can MEDIAN take both?
MEDIAN accepts several ranges separated by commas, and finds the middle of all the numbers combined. Do not take the median of two medians.
Type =MEDIAN(B2:B5,D2:D5) in F2 and press Enter. The eight days in order have 110 and 120 in the middle, so the median is 115.
steps.explanation: MEDIAN across two ranges treats all eight days as one list.

common_mistakes.message: That adds two medians, 235. Find the median of all the days together.
AVERAGE gives 116.875. MEDIAN gives the middle.
That covers Shop A only. Add Shop B as a second range.

title: MODE Function
objectives: By the end you can find the most frequent value in a list and compare the mean, median and mode.
about: The mode is the value that appears most often in a list. Excel's MODE function finds it. It looks at numbers only and ignores text and blank cells. Use it to find the most common shoe size, the most frequent score, or the usual delivery time. If two values tie, MODE returns the one that appears first in the list. If no value repeats, MODE shows #N/A. To use it, type =MODE(, select the cells, close the bracket, and press Enter. Compare it with the average and the median to see how the data is spread.

examples.scenario: A shoe shop finds its most common size.
examples.why: Size 9 appears twice, more than any other.

examples.scenario: A teacher finds the most common score and ignores absentees.
examples.why: The text is skipped.

examples.scenario: A courier finds the usual time across two lists.
examples.why: The tie between 30 and 45 goes to the value that appears first.

examples.scenario: An analyst shows mean, median and mode together.
examples.why: The mode is the most repeated value.

watch_out: If two values tie, MODE returns the first one in the list. If nothing repeats, it shows #N/A.
MODE works on numbers only. It cannot find the most common word.
Mean, median and mode can all differ. One extreme value moves the mean, but the median and mode stay put.
recap: You can now describe a list with total, count, average, extremes, median and mode. Next, Track 04 turns to decisions with IF.

steps.prompt: A shoe shop's sold sizes are in B2:B9. In D2, show the size sold most often, so the shop knows what to restock.
hints: You want the value that appears most often. Which function finds it?
MODE(range) returns the number that appears most often in the range. It is useful for sizes, ratings and other repeated values.
Type =MODE(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. Size 9 was sold three times, more than any other, so the answer is 9.
steps.explanation: MODE counts how often each number appears and returns the most frequent one.

common_mistakes.message: MEDIAN gives the middle size, 8.5. MODE gives the most frequent.
AVERAGE gives 8.375, which is not even a real size. MODE gives the most frequent.
MAX gives the largest size, 10. MODE gives the most frequent.

steps.prompt: Exam scores are in B2:B9, and one student is marked absent in text. In D2, show the most common score.
hints: MODE only looks at numbers. What happens to the text absent?
MODE ignores text and blank cells, so absent is skipped. Give it the whole score range, and it finds the most repeated number.
Type =MODE(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. The score 70 appears three times, and 85 appears twice, so the answer is 70.
steps.explanation: MODE skips the text and returns the most repeated score.

common_mistakes.message: AVERAGE gives 75.7. MODE gives the most frequent score.
MAX gives the top score, 90. MODE gives the most frequent.
COUNT gives how many scores there are, 7. MODE gives the most frequent.

steps.prompt: Morning delivery times are in B2:B5 and evening times in D2:D5. In F2, show the most common delivery time across both lists.
hints: The two lists must be looked at together. How can MODE take both?
MODE accepts several ranges separated by commas, and finds the most repeated number across all of them. Neither list alone gives the right answer.
Type =MODE(B2:B5,D2:D5) in F2 and press Enter. The time 30 appears three times across the lists, so the answer is 30.
steps.explanation: MODE with two ranges counts repeats across both lists together.

common_mistakes.message: That looks at the evening list only and gives 45. Add the morning list.
That looks at the morning list only. Add the evening list.
MEDIAN gives the middle time, 37.5. MODE gives the most frequent.

steps.prompt: Order sizes are in B2:B9. In D2, show a sentence such as Most common size: 38, built from the most common size.
hints: A sentence needs words and a number joined together. Which symbol joins them?
The & symbol joins text. Put the words in quotation marks, ending with a space, and join MODE after them so the number follows.
Type ="Most common size: "&MODE(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. Size 38 appears three times, so the sentence ends with 38.
steps.explanation: MODE supplies the number and & joins it to the words, so the sentence stays up to date.

common_mistakes.message: That shows only the number, 38. Join it to the words with &.
The number ran into the colon. End the words with a space.
That typed sentence will not update. Build it from MODE.

steps.prompt: Daily visitors Monday to Sunday are in B2:B8, and Sunday had an unusually big crowd. In D2, show a sentence in the form Mean 4, median 2, mode 2 so readers see all three measures.
hints: You need three functions in one sentence. Which symbol joins them together?
Join text and results with &. Use AVERAGE, MEDIAN and MODE for the three numbers, and put the labels and commas in quotation marks between them.
Type ="Mean "&AVERAGE(B2:B8)&", median "&MEDIAN(B2:B8)&", mode "&MODE(B2:B8) in D2. The result reads Mean 4, median 2, mode 2.
steps.explanation: Each function supplies a number and & joins it to its label. The outlier of 14 pulls the mean up, but the median and mode stay at 2.

common_mistakes.message: The mode is missing. Add it at the end.
The commas are missing. Add a comma and a space before each label.
That typed sentence will not update. Build it from the functions.

title: Track 03 Checkpoint: Summaries that matter
about: Three problems, one per level. Passing a level unlocks the next. Easy has hints on, Medium offers a hint only after a wrong attempt, and Hard has no hints.

steps.prompt: A chain's eight stores' sales are in B2:B9. In D2, work out the total sales.
hints: A total adds a whole list. Which function adds a range of cells?
SUM(range) adds every number in the range. B2:B9 runs from the first store to the last.
Type =SUM(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. The eight stores add up to 1100.
steps.explanation: SUM adds the whole range B2:B9 in one step.

common_mistakes.message: Hull is missing. The range must reach B9.
COUNT gives how many stores there are, 8. SUM adds their sales.
That adds only two stores. Use SUM with the whole range.

steps.prompt: Eight students' scores are in B2:B9, and two are marked n/a. In D2, work out the average score, using the real scores only.
hints: The text n/a is not a score. How does AVERAGE treat text in a range?
AVERAGE ignores text and blank cells, so n/a is left out of both the total and the count. Give it the whole range.
Type =AVERAGE(B2:B9) in D2 and press Enter. The six real scores add to 480, and 480 divided by 6 is 80.
steps.explanation: AVERAGE skips the n/a text, so it divides by the 6 real scores.

common_mistakes.message: That divides by all 8 rows, including n/a. AVERAGE counts only real scores.
COUNTA counts the n/a text as well. Use AVERAGE.
MEDIAN gives the middle score, not the average.

steps.prompt: Eight reps' sales are in B2:B9. In D2, work out the average of the three highest sales.
steps.explanation: The curly brackets ask LARGE for the first, second and third largest values at once. AVERAGE then averages 520, 500 and 480 to give 500.

common_mistakes.message: That averages only the third largest, 480. Use {1,2,3} for the top three.
SUM adds the top three, 1500. AVERAGE finds their average.
That averages every sale. You need only the top three.
